newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Big growth seen in Australia food exports to Asia.
newsitem.headline: Big growth seen in Australia food exports to Asia.

text.p: Australian agri-food exports to Asia would jump to almost US$20 billion a year by 2005 from about $8 billion in 1995 if it maintained present market share, a Agri-summit conference here was told.

Conservative estimates suggested Asia's agri-food imports could continue to grow by at least 10 percent a year, said Paul Tighe, assistant secretary (agriculture and resources), trade negotiations and organisations division, Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
Asia's agri-food imports totalled about $110 billion in 1995, with Australia commanding a a six to seven percent share, he said.
Conservatively-estimated growth of 10 percent a year would produce total Asian agri-food imports of more than $285 billion a year by 2005, he saod.
"Even if Australia were able only to maintain its present market share, its food exports to Asia would rise to almost $20 billion a year by 2005," he said.
Australia's natural resources gave it a strong comparative advantage in many bulk commodities, while its proximity to the Asian market gave it a particular advantage, he said.
"There are enormous potential opportunities for Australia's agri-food exports," he said.

Australia's substantial fresh food exports, such as meat and horticultural products, were particularly susceptible to being kept out of export markets on excessively onerous quarantine or technical grounds, he said.
But implementation of the Uruguay Round agreement on agriculture could increase the value of Australia's rural exports by as much as A$1 billion a year, he also said.

Potential benefits throughout the agriculture and food sector included a possible increase in beef exports estimated at A$330 million as year, while wheat exports could rise by A$320 million, dairy by A$210 million, coarse grains by A$50 million, rice by A$30 million and sugar by A$10 million, he said.

Australia's immediate tasks included extending regional trade liberalisation through the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) forum's individual action plan and through its sectoral liberalisation initiative, he said.
Early gains in the agri-food sector included an undertaking by Hong Kong that it would relax import controls on rice by 1997 and on meat and poultry by 2000, he said.

They also included an undertaking by Japan to revise administrative arrangements to facilitate entry of plant and animal imports and an undertaking by Korea to liberalise shelf-life restruictions by 1998, he said.
Australia had nominated the food sector as a target area for early sectoral liberalisation within APEC, he said.
